title: Annotatio I §.II close: Real dispute — propositions proper (Lutherans) or improper (Reformed/Gomarus) — stop before §.III
pass_a_gloss: In the same place, after he had needlessly added some things on the literal sense of the words viewed outside the proposition — i.e. on their propriety, never not to be conceded to the Reformed — and had even asserted, against the whole mind of the Reformers, that they want the literal sense of the Sacred Supper’s words retained by them opposed only to the mystical or allegorical, whereas they want that opposite to every false and less genuine sense, or to whatever abhors from the mind of speaking Christ and His immediate intention, he spontaneously acknowledges that every dispute on the literal sense of the Supper’s words retained or less retained, which Protestants agitate among themselves, recurs hither: Whether the words (namely as they complete Christ’s proposition) This is my body are to be taken properly, or rather improperly? The difference, he says, (between us and the Calvinists) in this place is that the Calvinists recede from the propriety of the words where they ought not, while the remaining opinion confesses that it follows and presses the Letter: Wherefore of the Sacred Supper’s words This is my Body, This is my blood (namely insofar as the several words are not considered in themselves — for so far their proper signification is never to be stripped or deprived by any of the Reformers — but insofar as they complete Christ’s whole proposition, on whose propriety and impropriety the controversy turns) the ῥητόν, letter, or literal sense is (namely for Lutherans) when all those words are left in their proper significations and there is no departure to a trope, whichever it finally be. p. 19 at the end & 20. Thus the Lutherans have the Reformed consenting, since the Reformed deny only this: that Christ’s words, as they constitute the proposition and obtain their literal, true, genuine sense — i.e. exactly answering the mind of speaking Christ — according to the common rule for an improper and a proper proposition, are taken properly. Or, that I may speak more clearly: these Propositions This is my Body and this is my blood (accepted in their literal, i.e. genuine and true sense) the Reformed deny to be proper (see Gomarus, Tom. 3, Disp. 35, thesis 10), which conversely the Lutherans contend to be proper — otherwise here distinguished, or to be distinguished, from the Reformed by no difference at all.
pass_b_english: After needless talk of word-propriety outside the proposition — which the Reformed never refuse — Schmidius himself grants that the whole Protestant fight over a retained or less-retained “literal” sense of the Supper words comes back to one question: as they complete Christ’s proposition, are This is my body taken properly or improperly?

For Lutherans the ῥητόν of This is my Body / This is my blood (as one whole proposition, not the several words stripped of their own proper sense) is when every word stays in its proper signification and no trope is admitted.

The Reformed deny only that those propositions, taken in their genuine literal sense, are proper (Gomarus, Tom. 3, Disp. 35, th. 10); Lutherans contend they are — otherwise the two sides would not differ here at all.
Stop before §. III (Reformed proofs that the definitive Supper propositions are improper — generic/specific arguments).
source_text: Ibidem, postquam de literali sensu verborum, extra propositionem spectatorum, i. e. de horum proprietate, Reformatis nunquam non concedenda, frustraque quaedam subjecisset, etiam, contra omnem Reformatorum mentem, asseruisset, eos literalem verborum S. Coenae sensum, à se retentum, mystico solì seu allegorico oppositum velle, cùm hunc oppositum velint omni falso minusque genuino, vel cuivis à mente loquentis Christi & huius immediata intentione, abhorrenti, sponte suâ agnoscit, omnem disputationem de sensu literali verborum Coenae retento, vel minùs retento, quam Protestantes inter se agitant, huc recurrere: An verba (prout nempe propositionem Christi absolvunt) Hoc est corpus meum, propriè, an verò impropriè, capienda sint? Discrimen, inquit, (inter nos & Calvinianos) hôc loco est illud quod Calviniani à proprietate verborum, ubi non deberent, recedunt, reliquae vero sententiae Literam se sequi & premere confitentur: Quare verborum S. Coenae Hoc est Corpus meum, Hoc est sanguis meus (puta quatenus non singula in se verba considerantur, utpote eatenus propria sua significatione à Reformatorum nemine exuenda privandaque unquam, sed quatenus integram Christi propositionem conficiunt, de cujus proprietate & improprietate controvertitur) ῥητόν, litera, seu literalis sensus, is est (scil. Lutheranis) cùm verba ista omnia in propriis suis significationibus relinquuntur, nec ad tropum, quicunque ille tandem sit, disceditur. p. 19. in fin. & 20. Sic verò Reformatos Lutherani habent consentientes, cum hoc solùm negent Reformati: Verba Christi prout propositionem constituunt, sensumque suum literalem, verum genuinum, i. e. menti dicentis Christi exactè respondentem, propositioni impropriae propriaeque juxta communem, obtinent, propriè accipi. Vel, ut clariùs loquar: Propositiones has: Hoc est Corpus meum, & hic est sanguis meus, (in literali i. e. genuino veroque sensu suo acceptas) proprias negant esse Reformati (Vid. Gom. Tom. 3. Diff. 35. thes. 10.) quas vice versâ proprias contendunt Lutherani, alioquin, nullô omnino discrimine hîc à Reformatis distincti, vel distinguendi.

lemmas.gloss: to be taken properly or improperly
